one_liner: Toy NASM AVX/AVX-512/rep movsb copy loops timed against libc memcpy on one huge buffer; not a usable memcpy.
what_it_does: A small benchmark (memcpy_bench.c) that times libc memcpy against three NASM routines with the memcpy signature: memcpy_avx256, memcpy_avx512 and a three-instruction memcpy_movsb. Each mode copies one fresh 512 MiB (now 128 MiB) heap buffer 11 times and checks the result with memcmp. A later mode 5 splits the copy over 4 pthreads (libs/memcpy_multithread.c); the AVX files are generated by gen_avx_memcpy.php.
how_it_is_fast: The AVX routines are fully unrolled block copies: 16 ymm loads then 16 ymm stores per 512-byte block (AVX-256), or 32 zmm per 2048-byte block (AVX-512; 16 zmm per 1024-byte block in the version that was timed), each block preceded by prefetcht1 on every source and destination line. memcpy_movsb is just rep movsb, relying on the CPU's ERMS microcode. There is no alignment handling, no non-temporal stores and no size dispatch.
when_to_use: As a reading example of how an unrolled AVX/AVX-512 register-block copy and a bare rep movsb compare on very large buffers.
As a starting harness for your own large-copy experiments, after fixing the averaging and page-fault issues listed under gotchas.
Only memcpy_movsb is safe to lift as-is (any length, returns dst); it suits large copies on CPUs with ERMS/FSRM.
when_not_to_use: As a drop-in memcpy: memcpy_avx256 and memcpy_avx512 are correct only for non-zero lengths that are exact multiples of 512 and 2048 bytes; any other length overruns both buffers (see gotchas).
Small or medium copies: there is no small-size path, and every call issues at least one full 512- or 2048-byte block.
Non-x86-64 targets, or the AVX-512 routine on CPUs without AVX-512F (it faults with an illegal instruction; the harness has no CPUID check).
When you need a measured win: on the AMD A8 rep movsb alone matches the AVX routine, and on the Xeon the author's own earlier run with identical AVX-256 code tied libc.
Production use of the multithreaded mode: memcpy_mt_exec drops the len % 4 tail and coordinates workers with plain bools and unfair mutex hand-offs.

integration.dependencies: nasm (to assemble the .asm files); pthreads only for the multithreaded mode
integration.min_toolchain: nasm with AVX-512 support and any C compiler; versions not documented (result commit built the harness with gcc -Wall -O0)
integration.platforms: x86-64 System V (Linux ELF64); AVX for memcpy_avx256, AVX-512F for memcpy_avx512, ERMS recommended for memcpy_movsb
integration.thread_safety: Single-threaded routines are reentrant (no state); the multithreaded wrapper uses global state and unsynchronised bool flags, so it is not safe to call concurrently
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — memcpy_movsb is a valid memcpy; memcpy_avx256/memcpy_avx512 only work for non-zero lengths that are multiples of 512/2048 bytes and return src instead of dst

gotchas: Correctness bug in both AVX routines (and in the gen_avx_memcpy.php generator): the size dispatch is 'cmp rcx, 512' followed by an unconditional 'jmp .jge_512' (not jge), and it compares the running offset rcx rather than the remaining length rdx. Every iteration therefore copies a full 512-byte (AVX-512: 2048-byte) block and loops until rdx reaches exactly zero; for any length that is not a non-zero multiple of the block size, rdx wraps negative and the loop runs past both buffers until it faults. The benchmark's 128/512 MiB buffers are exact multiples, so its memcmp check passes and hides the bug.

Both AVX routines start with 'mov rax, rsi', so they return the source pointer, not dst as memcpy must; neither executes vzeroupper before returning, so callers' later SSE code can pay AVX-SSE transition penalties.

Harness flaws behind result.txt: 11 timed copies are averaged over 10 (every Avg exceeds its Max); each copy writes to a freshly malloc'd, never-touched destination, so roughly 131,072 first-touch page faults per 512 MiB run are inside the timed region (derived copy rates of only about 1.5-2.0 GB/s on the Xeon); timing uses gettimeofday. At the result commits the Makefile built the harness with 'gcc -Wall -O0', not the -O3 now in the Makefile (the libc memcpy baseline is prebuilt, so this does not change it).

The Xeon headline is not stable: result.txt at commits 8be9917 and a955014 (same memcpy_bench.c, Makefile and byte-identical memcpy_avx256.asm) recorded libc min 0.3486 s vs AVX-256 min 0.3464 s (a tie; AVX avg 0.3844 vs libc 0.3838) on the same Xeon 8269CY VM; commit 7d431e0 replaced it with the current libc 0.3494 vs AVX-256 0.2711 s (1.29x). The AVX-512 row was also measured on two different routines (1024-byte blocks, then 2048-byte blocks). The AMD A8 rows were consistent across runs (about 1.2x for both AVX and rep movsb).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only to study block-unrolled AVX copies versus rep movsb at the 512 MiB scale; for a usable faster memcpy, FastMemcpy (skywind3000) has real size dispatch and covers small and medium sizes, and asmlib (abiiranathan) benchmarks against a stated glibc 2.44.
verified_claims_summary: On an Intel Xeon Platinum 8269CY cloud VM, one 512 MiB single-threaded copy took min 0.2711 s with the AVX-256 routine versus 0.3494 s with the prebuilt libc memcpy (glibc version unknown), about 1.29x, with AVX-512 at 0.2854 s and rep movsb at 0.3020 s; on an AMD A8-6410 the AVX routine and plain rep movsb both ran at about 0.445 s versus 0.546 s for libc (about 1.2x). Timings include first-touch page faults on the destination, and an earlier run of the same AVX-256 code on the same Xeon showed no gain over libc.
status_note: Abandoned since 2020-09-22 (24 commits in four days, no issues or releases) and Unlicense public domain, but the AVX routines have an out-of-bounds bug for any length that is not a non-zero multiple of 512/2048 bytes, so treat it as reference material rather than copyable code; only the rep movsb routine is safe to reuse.
